Benchmarking World-Model Learning

Archana Warrier Affiliation: Basis Research Institute Affiliation: DFKI GmbH    Thanh Dat Nguyen Affiliation: Basis Research Institute Affiliation: Harvard University    Michelangelo Naim Affiliation: Basis Research Institute    Moksh Jain Affiliation: Basis Research Institute Affiliation: Université de Montréal & Mila - Quebec AI Institute    Yichao Liang Affiliation: Basis Research Institute Affiliation: University of Cambridge    Karen Schroeder Affiliation: Basis Research Institute    Cambridge Yang Affiliation: Basis Research Institute    Joshua B. Tenenbaum Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology    Sebastian Vollmer Affiliation: DFKI GmbH    Kevin Ellis Affiliation: Cornell University    Zenna Tavares Affiliation: Basis Research Institute
Abstract

Model-learning agents should gather information to learn world models that support many downstream tasks and inferences, such as predicting unobserved states, estimating near- and far-term consequences of actions, planning action sequences, and detecting changes in dynamics. Current methods for learning and evaluating world models diverge from this goal: training and evaluation are anchored to next-frame prediction, and success is scored by reward maximization in the same environment. We propose WorldTest, a protocol to evaluate model-learning agents that separates reward-free interaction from a scored test phase in a different but related environment. WorldTest is open-ended—models should support many different tasks unknown ahead of time—and agnostic to model representation, allowing comparison across approaches. We instantiated WorldTest with AutumnBench, a suite of 43 interactive grid-world environments and 129 tasks across three families: masked-frame prediction, planning, and predicting changes to the causal dynamics. We compared 517 human participants and three frontier models on AutumnBench. We found that humans outperform the models, and scaling compute improves performance only in some environments but not others. WorldTest provides a novel template—reward-free exploration, derived tests, and behavior-based scoring—to evaluate what agents learn about environment dynamics, and AutumnBench exposes significant headroom in world-model learning.

1 Introduction

Consider someone who cooks regularly in their own kitchen. Over time, they build an internal model of the workspace—where tools live and how appliances behave. That model supports various everyday capabilities. For example, it enables the person to: (1) Predict how long the hidden contents of a covered pot will take to finish cooking, based on steam intensity and elapsed time, (2) Recognize and adapt to changes when traveling and cooking in a short-term rental, where the kitchen is different (e.g., knives in a different drawer), and (3) Plan the sequence of actions to complete a set of recipes. Cognitive science refers to this flexible, predictive, and counterfactual understanding as world model (Weisberg & Gopnik, 2013), a core substrate of human intelligence.

Artificial intelligence research formalizes a world model as a representation of environment dynamics—most commonly a function mapping histories of states and actions to predictions of future states and rewards (Sutton & Barto, 2018). Many researchers argue that learning such models is pivotal for the next step in AI progress (LeCun & Courant, 2022).

A key component of world-model learning research is its evaluation. However, current evaluation methods are fragmented: some use non-interactive environments, others force models into specific structures or output formats, and still others reduce success solely to reward optimization.

Existing Approaches to World-Model Evaluation

We categorize approaches to evaluating world-model learning, detailed in Table 1, into four non-exclusive categories:

  • •

    Non-interactive benchmarks test whether agents can infer underlying rules from examples and generalize to novel test cases (Chollet, 2019; Depeweg et al., 2018; Barrett et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020; Yi et al., 2020a). These benchmarks are non-interactive, meaning they do not model environments that evolve over time or in response to actions.

  • •

    Representation-based approaches evaluate world models by requiring them to use specific, predefined formats—such as next-frame prediction, programs, or causal graphs—and assessing model performance using proxies within each representational format, for instance, measuring pixel-level reconstruction error for visual models (Kamada & Ichimura, 2024; Hu et al., 2024), using LLM-based evaluation for text-based models (Jansen et al., 2024), or requiring models to use high-level predicates (e.g., object relations or causal effects) and evaluating predicate prediction accuracy (Yi et al., 2020b; Girdhar & Ramanan, 2020; Ahmed et al., 2021). However, by mandating specific representational formats, these methods require a white-box model and prevent comparison between different model types or assessment against human performance. The reliance on potentially inadequate proxy measures further constrains evaluation, limiting our ability to assess world model capabilities across different agents in a meaningful way.

  • •

    Gym-like benchmarks resemble OpenAI Gym (Brockman et al., 2016) in that they model decision processes with explicit objectives such as rewards (Bellemare et al., 2013; Cobbe et al., 2019; Küttler et al., 2023; Samvelyan et al., 2021; Ahmed et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Tunyasuvunakool et al., 2020). However, these benchmarks evaluate performance on a specific environment’s task rather than directly assessing the quality of the world model itself.

  • •

    Unsupervised RL benchmarks goes beyond gym-like environments by evaluating agents using a two-phase protocol (Laskin et al., 2021). First, the agent interacts with a gym-like environment without an explicit objective. Then, the agent is tested with a downstream task in the same environment. Note that the “spot-the-difference in the kitchen” scenario mentioned above does not fit neatly into this category, as it requires evaluation in a modified environment only correlated with the original.

In this work, we aim to create a unifying framework for world-model learning by addressing the research question: How to design world-model evaluation frameworks and benchmarks that are (1) interactive, (2) behavior-based, meaning the framework treats the agent as a black-box and evaluates only by its external behavior, and (3) goal-free during interaction — similar to unsupervised RL benchmarks — yet (4) testing beyond the environment of interaction?

Our Approach

We introduce WorldTest, a representation-agnostic, behavior-based world-model evaluation framework that is goal-free in the base environment. It consists of two phases: interaction and test. In the interaction phase, the agent interacts with the base environment without external rewards. In the test phase, the framework transforms the base environment into a derived challenge environment with an explicit objective that differs from—but remains correlated with—the base. WorldTest evaluates the agent’s performance on the objective in this challenge environment.

WorldTest offers three advantages over existing methods: (1) WorldTest scores only an agent’s behavior, without inspecting or assuming anything about its internal representation, which makes the assessment applicable to any model representation. (2) The interaction phase is goal-free, i.e., the agent does not optimize any specific reward function, similar to prior unsupervised RL benchmarks (Laskin et al., 2021). (3) The test phase measures how well the agent uses its learned world model to solve a new, related challenge environment. Unlike previous approaches that restrict rewards in the original environment, this framework evaluates world-learning by introducing novel challenges. It can cover a broad range of world-model tests that were previously difficult, such as the “spot-the-difference-in-kitchen” example.

We further instantiate WorldTest by AutumnBench, a benchmark consisting of 43 grid-world environments and three types of challenges for each environment. The three challenges mirror the capabilities in our cooking example:

  • •

    Masked-frame prediction (MFP), where the agent infers unobserved parts of a final observation given a masked trajectory, analogous to predicting cooking completion time from partially observable information.

  • •

    Planning, where the agent acts to achieve a goal state, similar to sequencing recipe steps.

  • •

    Change detection (CD), where the agent identifies a change in the dynamics of the environment and reports the earliest timestep where the observation differs from the expected observation in the original environment, similar to recognizing changes in a different kitchen.

We provide 129 tasks across all environments that cover essential world-model skills, including prediction, planning, and counterfactual reasoning. These tasks are not exhaustive, and we designed AutumnBench to be extensible. Example extensions include new grid worlds with non-Newtonian physics or tests for tool reuse and analogical reasoning. For example, an agent might be tested to see if it can recognize that a wine bottle can substitute for a rolling pin when one is unavailable. Finally, we validate AutumnBench with an empirical study involving 517 humans and three state-of-the-art AI models, showing that it reveals the gap between AI and humans in world-model learning.

Contributions

We present the following contributions:

  • •

    We propose WorldTest, the first theoretical world-model learning assessment framework that is representation-agnostic, interaction-centric, and goal-free in the world-model-learning environment.

  • •

    We release AutumnBench, an instantiation of WorldTest with 43 interactive environments and three challenge families, resulting in 129 tasks. AutumnBench is designed following the desiderata for novel games outlined in Ying et al. (2025), is easily extensible, and supports automated evaluation for both human and AI models to accelerate progress in world-model learning.

  • •

    We evaluate 517 human participants and three state-of-the-art reasoning models (Anthropic Claude, OpenAI o3, and Google Gemini 2.5 Pro) on AutumnBench. We analyze their interaction trajectories and performance on challenge tasks, revealing substantial headroom for the reasoning models.

In the remainder of the paper, Section 2 provides background on the Autumn language, which is used for defining the environments, and the Partially Observed Markov Decision Process (POMDP) formulation of the environments in WorldTest and AutumnBench. Section 3 describes the core WorldTest framework and AutumnBench. Section 4 presents evaluations and analysis of the baseline agents on AutumnBench. Finally, Section 5 concludes and discusses future work.

2 Background

This section provides background on the POMDP formulation of the environments in AutumnBench and Autumn, as well as the language used to implement these POMDP environments.

Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs).

We formulate environments as (reward-free) POMDPs. A POMDP is a tuple ⟨𝒮,𝒜,𝒪,𝒯,Ω⟩\langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{O},\mathcal{T},\Omega\rangle, where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the (hidden) state space, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the action space, 𝒪\mathcal{O} is the observation space, 𝒯:𝒮×𝒜→Δ⁡(𝒮)\mathcal{T}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\Delta(\mathcal{S}) is the transition function that maps state-action pairs to a distribution over the next states , and Ω:𝒮×𝒜→Δ⁡(𝒪)\Omega:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\Delta(\mathcal{O}) is the observation function that maps from a state-action pairs to a distribution over observations. An agent interacts with the environment by choosing actions and receiving an observation at each step.

The Autumn Language.

We implement the POMDP environments in AutumnBench using the Autumn domain-specific language (DSL). Autumn is a functional reactive language for specifying causal interactions in 2D grids, introduced in Das et al. (2023). We chose Autumn as the language for AutumnBench because it allows for succinct and expressive specification of the environments, is easy to extend to implement downstream challenges, and supports both a text-based Gym-like interface for evaluating AI agents and a browser-based graphical user interface for evaluating human agents. We provide a detailed description of the Autumn language in Appendix A.

3 Theoretical Framework and Benchmark

We introduce WorldTest, a behavior-based framework that evaluates an agent’s ability to infer and use models of the environment. We then present an instantiation of WorldTest, AutumnBench, as a suite of 43 environments written in the Autumn language, with three types of challenges for each environment. The following sections describe the WorldTest framework and its realization in AutumnBench.

3.1 WorldTest Framework

We first outline the intuition of the framework and then provide a formal definition.

Intuition.

We design WorldTest to evaluate world-model learning without constraining either the agent’s internal representation or the agent’s reward. To this end, WorldTest follows a two-phase protocol that assesses the agent purely through its behavior:

  1. 1.

    Interaction phase: The agent interacts autonomously with the environment, selecting actions without objectives or external rewards. During this phase, the agent can reset the environment to its initial state as many times as needed to facilitate hypothesis testing and systematic exploration. The phase ends when the agent elects to proceed to the next.

  2. 2.

    Test phase: The evaluation protocol presents a challenge environment derived from the original by modifying one or more POMDP components, such as states, transitions, or actions. These environments add explicit rewards or goals, unlike the earlier reward-free phase. They test whether an agent’s learned world model can generalize across different aspects of understanding the environment. The agent must act in the challenge environment to achieve the stated objective.

We give the formal definition of this framework below.

Formal Definition.

Let ℳ=⟨S,A,O,T,Ω⟩\mathcal{M}=\langle S,A,O,T,\Omega\rangle denote the reward-free base environment whose dynamics are unknown to the agent. Let Ξ\Xi be a task parameter space with associated distribution PΞP_{\Xi}. A WorldTest evaluation protocol consists of PΞP_{\Xi} and a deterministic function

τ:(ℳ,ξ)↦(ℳ′,R,H)\tau:(\mathcal{M},\xi)\mapsto(\mathcal{M}^{\prime},R,H)

where ξ∼PΞ\xi\sim P_{\Xi} is a task parameter, ℳ′=⟨S′,A′,O′,T′,Ω′⟩\mathcal{M}^{\prime}=\langle S^{\prime},A^{\prime},O^{\prime},T^{\prime},\Omega^{\prime}\rangle is a derived challenge environment, R:(O′×A)H→ℝR:(O^{\prime}\times A)^{H}\to\mathbb{R} is an objective function, and H∈ℕH\in\mathbb{N} is the evaluation horizon. The challenge environment ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} differs from ℳ\mathcal{M} through modifications to the state space, dynamics, observations, or the addition of rewards. Different definitions of τ\tau correspond to different task types (for example, masked frame prediction, planning, and change detection in AutumnBench).

We describe a concrete run of the protocol by detailing the actions of both the protocol and the agent at each step. Given an environment ℳ\mathcal{M} and a protocol (τ\tau, PΞP_{\Xi}), the evaluation proceeds as follows:

  1. Step 1.

    Step 1. Disclose task type. The protocol informs the agent of the task type by describing τ\tau, which reveals the challenge action space A′A^{\prime}, the challenge observation space O′O^{\prime}, and the form of the reward function RR (e.g., binary success criteria or continuous rewards with penalties). The protocol does not disclose the task parameters Ξ\Xi, the modified dynamics (T′,Ω′)(T^{\prime},\Omega^{\prime}), the explicit reward targets, or any actual observations from ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime}.

  2. Step 2.

    Step 2. Interact with the environment. The agent explores ℳ\mathcal{M} without external rewards, interacting freely with the environment. At any time, the agent may reset the environment to its initial state or proceed to the test phase. During this phase, the agent collects an interaction history and constructs an internal model ℳ^\widehat{\mathcal{M}} that generalizes to the challenge action and observation spaces A′A^{\prime} and O′O^{\prime} for the given τ\tau.

  3. Step 3.

    Instantiate the protocol. When the agent decides to go to the test, the protocol samples task parameters ξ∼PΞ\xi\sim P_{\Xi} and computes (ℳ′,R,H)=τ⁡(ℳ,ξ)(\mathcal{M}^{\prime},R,H)=\tau(\mathcal{M},\xi).

  4. Step 4.

    Produce a policy from the internal model. Using its internal model ℳ^\widehat{\mathcal{M}} and knowledge of τ\tau, the agent returns a policy π:(O′)∗→Δ⁡(A)\pi:(O^{\prime})^{*}\to\Delta(A).

  5. Step 5.

    Execute the policy in the challenge environment. The agent runs π\pi in ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} for HH steps, obtaining a history h′=(o0′,a0′,…,oH′,aH′)h^{\prime}=(o^{\prime}_{0},a^{\prime}_{0},\ldots,o^{\prime}_{H},a^{\prime}_{H}).

  6. Step 6.

    Score. The protocol computes the score R⁡(h′)R(h^{\prime}).

The interaction phase imposes no time limit, but agents only receive scores if they complete the test. While, in theory, an agent might interact indefinitely, WorldTest conditions evaluation on agents eventually moving on to testing. In practice, however, finite resources prevent indefinite exploration.

3.2 AutumnBench: Design and Implementation

In this section, we present an instantiation of the WorldTest framework, namely, AutumnBench. We instantiate WorldTest by implementing three τ\tau functions for three task-types: masked frame prediction (τMFP\tau_{\text{MFP}}), planning (τPL\tau_{\text{PL}}), and change detection (τCD\tau_{\text{CD}}). AutumnBench consists of 129 problems. Each problem in AutumnBench has two parts: (1) a base environment with no rewards that the agent interacts with in the interaction phase, and (2) a related challenge environment for the test phase.

We describe each of those parts in more detail below, beginning with the environments used in the interaction phase and followed by the related challenge tasks for the test phase:

Interaction-Phase Environments.

Each AutumnBench environment is a grid world composed of objects, represented as collections of pixels, along with their dynamics. We define these dynamics programmatically in AutumnBench environments using the Autumn DSL (Das et al., 2023).

The grid sizes of these environments range from 3×33\times 3 to 25×2525\times 25, with most at 16×1616\times 16. Each environment includes about five or fewer object types and 1 to 12 colors, with 19 of the 43 environments being stochastic. Table B.1 summarizes the complexity metrics across all environments. Our environments meet the three novel game desiderata from Ying et al. (2025) for evaluating world model learning: they are structurally novel, intuitive to humans, and diverse in both world dynamics and learning mechanisms. Figure 1 illustrates sample environments. AutumnBench includes Atari-like games (Bellemare et al., 2013), simulations of real-world phenomena like plant growth and sandcastle construction, and strategic games like Nim (Wikipedia, 2025). Appendix B provides further details on the different classes of environments in AutumnBench.

Test-Phase Challenges.

We selected the test-phase challenges to address various aspects of existing world model evaluations. Specifically, AutumnBench implements the test phase of WorldTest by assessing the agent through the following three types of challenges:

  • •

    Masked Frame Prediction (MFP): The agent observes a trajectory with partially masked frames and predicts the missing content in the final frame by selecting from six options, only one of which matches the ground truth. The agent receives a score of 1 for a correct selection and 0 otherwise.

  • •

    Planning: The protocol gives the agent a goal that specifies a target state for a subgrid, and the agent is required to generate a sequence of actions to reach that target state. The agent is scored 1 or 0 based on whether or not it reaches the target state.

  • •

    Change Detection (CD): The agent interacts with a modified version of the base environment in which a rule changes dynamically. It must identify the timestep when the change is triggered. Agents receive full scores for detecting the change at the correct time; late detection incurs penalties, and selecting a timestep before the change results in a score of zero.

In AutumnBench, we implement Step 1 of the WorldTest protocol in Section 3.1 using interface-specific means: interactive tutorials for humans and text descriptions for reasoning models, further described in Section 4. However, the agents does not learn the specific task parameters ξ\xi at this stage, such as which frames are masked, when the change occurs, or what the designated goal states are.

We detail the formulation of each challenge and environment in Appendix C.

4 Baseline Evaluations and Analysis

We evaluate humans and reasoning models on AutumnBench using the two-phase WorldTest framework. Human participants are recruited via Prolific (Prolific, 2025). For model baselines, we use Claude 4 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and o3. Section 4.1 details the evaluation setup for both.

We analyze agents’ performance, exploration strategies during the interaction phase, and the impact of computational resources across AutumnBench tasks in Section 4.2. We then discuss these results, as well as their implications in Section 4.3.

4.1 Evaluation Setup

In this section, we describe how we tested agents on AutumnBench, including participant selection and filtering criteria, as well as the implementation details of the interface for each agent.

4.1.1 Human Evaluation

We recruited 517 English-speaking participants via Prolific. To ensure the quality of our sample, we included only individuals who were not color blind and who successfully passed both attention and comprehension checks (Muszyński, 2023). We repeated each problem 20 times and distributed them uniformly across participants.

Having recruited our sample as described above, we aimed to measure the performance of a single baseline agent representing the average human who engages seriously with the task rather than to evaluate individual variation. As crowd-sourced responses exhibited high variability despite screening measures (Reid et al., 2022; Douglas et al., 2023), often reflecting differences in effort and engagement rather than cognitive capability, we constructed this agent by taking the 80th percentile score per problem across the 20 human attempts. Throughout our analysis, “human” performance refers to this single 80th-percentile aggregate agent.

We implemented AutumnBench using a web-based graphical user interface (GUI) for the human participants. We provided each participant with a tutorial that taught them how to navigate the GUI for their assigned task type. The tutorial describes the τ\tau being used, i.e., τMFP\tau_{\text{MFP}}, τPlanning\tau_{\text{Planning}}, or τCD\tau_{\text{CD}}, which corresponds to Step 1 of the WorldTest protocol in Section 3.1. Figure 1 shows a rendered grid and GUI buttons for reset and go-to-test actions during the interaction phase.

The GUI updates the grid at a fixed, environment-dependent frame rate, ranging from 3 to 8 frames per second (FPS), creating real-time experiences that mimic natural exploration. Participants engage using directional arrow keys or by clicking on grid cells at each timestep. If they do not act within the timestep, the interface automatically updates the grid state using no-op. The interface for the masked frame prediction, planning, and change detection tasks includes interactive features shown in Figure 1. Section D.2.1 gives the GUI implementation details for each task type.

4.1.2 Reasoning-Model Evaluation

We evaluated three frontier reasoning models—Claude 4 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and o3—on AutumnBench. We gave one AutumnBench problem to each model at a time. Due to cost constraints, we evaluated each model’s performance based on a single trajectory completion per problem.

At every timestep, we provide each model with complete interaction histories, current grid state, available actions, and a description of the task-type (i.e., which τ\tau function is being applied) corresponding to Step 1 of the WorldTest protocol in Section 3.1. We represent grid states as two-dimensional arrays of color strings, see Figure 2.

We evaluated three frontier reasoning models—Claude 4 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and o3—on AutumnBench. We gave one AutumnBench problem to each model at a time. Due to cost constraints, we evaluated each model’s performance based on a single trajectory completion per problem.

While humans have an implicit time limit to take actions, due to the fixed frame rate, the reasoning models are allowed to step through the environment without any time limit. The model can still choose not to take any action in the environment through a no-op. Similar to humans, during the interaction phase, the models can select the go-to-test action to transition to the test phase and the reset action to reset the grid to its initial state. Section D.2.2 describes the implementation details for each task type.

4.2 Results

We analyze agent behavior on AutumnBench in three areas: task performance, exploration patterns, and world-model learning over time. We first compare agent scores across environments and tasks. Next, we examine how exploration strategies adopted by the agents affect task performance. Finally, we analyze the emergence of focused behavior as agents build their world models.

4.2.1 Overall Performance

In this section, we present our comparative performance results and examine the factors that enable reasoning models to perform better. Humans outperformed all reasoning models across all environments, as shown in Figure 4. Table E.1 shows detailed scores for each agent and task type, and Figure 6(a) shows environment-wise score distributions.

To understand what factors contribute to the performance of reasoning models, we first examined how environmental stochasticity affects different agents. Humans maintained nearly identical performance in both deterministic and stochastic environments. Reasoning models, however, performed significantly better in stochastic settings than in deterministic settings, as shown in Figure 4.

Next, we examined the impact of computational cost on model performance. We identified two sets, A and B, of AutumnBench environments that scale better and worse as the cost increases, respectively. In particular, performance improved with higher computational cost in 25 of 43 environments, i.e., SetA, and remained flat or decreased in 18, i.e., SetB, as shown in Figure 3. We detail these two sets in Appendix D. At the task level, increased cost improved performance in 37% of masked frame prediction and planning environments, but only 33% for change detection. In some environments, average performance consistently improved with additional resources across all task types, while others showed no improvement, regardless of task type, highlighting the need for better agents. Appendix E provides environment-specific analyses.

4.2.2 Exploration Patterns

We analyze the actions that agents take during exploration with two complementary methods. First, we analyze the distribution of unique actions by counting each distinct click position and directional action separately. For example, clicking on positions (2,3)(2,3) and (5,7)(5,7) counts as two unique click actions. This approach allows us to account for environment-specific variations, such as differences in static object positions and grid sizes within AutumnBench. We then calculate the fraction of unique actions in each category—clicks, directional actions, reset, and no-op—relative to the total number of unique actions performed by the agent, as shown in Figure 5. Humans use roughly equal proportions of resets and no-ops at 12.5% each, while reasoning models focus on clicks and directional actions. All reasoning models use less than 7% of their actions for resets and no-ops combined. Claude uses 98.6% for clicks and arrows. Among reasoning models, o3 uses the highest fraction for resets and no-ops at 11.5%, while Claude uses the lowest at 2.1%.

Second, we examine agents’ reset frequencies. Figure 6(d) shows humans reset more often than models, which reset less often and with greater variance. Both analyses suggest that reasoning models do not treat resets as special actions, unlike humans. Table E.2 summarizes average actions per environment.

4.2.3 World-Model Learning

We quantify how agents acquire world models by measuring how their actions become more focused over time. Specifically, we use normalized perplexity, which we define in Definition D.1, to quantify how predictable an agent’s actions are while exploring. High perplexity suggests actions are random, while low perplexity suggests more targeted behavior.

We analyze normalized perplexity across the entire interaction sequence using two metrics. The Area Under the Curve (AUC) of normalized perplexity, as defined in Definition D.2, captures the overall learning trajectory. Agents that quickly develop focused exploration strategies show lower AUC values. Final perplexity measures how targeted agents become by the end of exploration. Both metrics are robust to brief fluctuations and enable fair comparison across environments and agents.

Humans show lower values on both measures, as seen in Figures 6(b) and 6(c), suggesting more effective world model learning. Lower AUC values indicate that they rapidly transition from random clicks and keypresses to more targeted actions. Their final normalized perplexity values are consistently lower than those of reasoning models, suggesting more deterministic and purposeful behavior by the end of the exploration. Figure 6 visualizes these trends across environments.

4.3 Discussion

Our results reveal differences in how humans and reasoning models approach world-model learning across two key dimensions: experimental design and belief updating.

Hypothesize and experiment.

We conjecture that humans use resets as experimental tools to test hypotheses about environmental dynamics. Reasoning models also form and test hypotheses, but their reasoning traces suggest a narrow view of what counts as informative actions, as illustrated in Appendix E. They prioritize keypresses and clicks, failing to recognize that resets and no-ops can be as or more valuable for testing hypotheses and generating additional observations. This limited view leads reasoning models to miss opportunities for more effective exploration.

Belief update.

Reasoning models often fail to update their understanding when faced with contradictory evidence, especially in masked frame prediction tasks; see Appendix E. Even when they recognize that test-phase observations contradict the rules learned during interaction, they tend to rely on those original rules in their predictions. This inflexibility highlights a limitation in meta-reasoning: reasoning models cannot determine when or how to revise what they have learned.

Collectively, these results demonstrate that humans outperform current reasoning models due to their limitations at several levels of inference. Rather than simply requiring better priors over world models, which most current training approaches focus on, our findings suggest that human-level performance requires advances in metacognitive capabilities: strategic experimental design, better uncertainty quantification, and flexible belief updating during exploration and task execution.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we present WorldTest, a representation-agnostic, behavior-based framework that separates a goal-free interaction phase from a scored test phase. By scoring only behavior in the derived challenges, WorldTest evaluates how agents apply their learned understanding to new tasks.

Instantiating WorldTest, AutumnBench has 43 environments and three derived challenge families, resulting in a total of 129 tasks. In doing so, AutumnBench replicates benchmarks for three facets of world modeling: next-frame prediction, causal change detection, and planning. It also enables cross-comparison and ablation within a single unified framework.

Our experiments with 517 human participants and three frontier reasoning models on AutumnBench demonstrated that humans outperform these models across all environments and task types, indicating substantial room for improvement in the world-modelling capabilities of current frontier models. Specifically, our analysis reveals that humans achieve near-optimal scores while existing models frequently fail. We also observed that human participants used the reset action far more often than the models and achieved lower perplexity over their trajectories than the models, suggesting a possible link between humans’ use of resets as an exploration or hypothesis-testing mechanism and their ability to refine internal models of the world during interaction better than reasoning models.

AutumnBench serves as a first step in using WorldTest to test different aspects of world model learning. While AutumnBench demonstrates WorldTest in a grid-world setting with simplified dynamics, WorldTest itself is a much broader framework. WorldTest can be further instantiated in physics-rich environments, robotics domains, and multi-agent systems, among other domains. The framework can accommodate existing physics-rich or embodied environments by treating them as base POMDPs and deriving challenge tasks beyond planning.

Reproducibility Statement

We provide a detailed description of the benchmark’s design, scoring methodology, and theoretical framework in Section 3 to facilitate the reproduction of our experiments and results by others. In Section 4.1, we describe the evaluation setup, agent interfaces, and procedures. The appendix contains the exact prompt template used for the reasoning-model agents. Our supplementary materials include: (1) Autumn source programs for all base environments and their derived challenges, and (2) Task specifications and answer keys where applicable. (3) The code implementing AutumnBench for reasoning models. The AutumnBench web-based GUI is publicly available at https://autumn.basis.ai. To protect the benchmark’s integrity and prevent data leakage, we keep a subset of AutumnBench problems private but provide full specifications for all reported experiments and for the publicly released problems.

Appendix A The Autumn Language

We implement the POMDP environments in AutumnBench using the Autumn domain-specific language (DSL). Autumn is a functional reactive language for specifying causal interactions in 2D grids, introduced in Das et al. (2023). We chose Autumn as the base language for AutumnBench because it allows succinct and expressive specification of environments, is easily extensible to implement downstream challenges, and supports both a text-based Gym-like interface for evaluating AI agents and a browser-based graphical user interface for evaluating human participants.

An Autumn program has the following parts:

  • •

    Environment setup defines the grid size (n×nn\times n) and background color.

  • •

    Object type definitions specify each object type by listing its shape (as relative 2D coordinates and colors) and its internal fields. These fields record state variables unique to each object instance.

  • •

    Object instance definitions define the initial state of each object instance and the default function for each object instance under the no-op action.

  • •

    Event handlers establish the rest of the full transition function TT. In particular, an on clause pairs a predicate p⁡(s,a)p(s,a) with an intervention ii, so that if p⁡(s,a)p(s,a) holds, the state transitions to s′=i⁡(s)s^{\prime}=i(s).

An Autumn program defines a POMDP. Specifically, the global variables in the program correspond to the hidden state. The agent observes only the grid’s color matrix (n×nn\times n), where every cell occupied by the highest-z-order object instance is visible; all other state components remain latent. The action space of an Autumn environment are: 1. the no-op action, 2. four directional actions—up, down, left, right—corresponding to the four arrow keys on a typical keyboard, and 3. a family of click actions click​(x,y)\text{click}(x,y), corresponding to clicking on the cell at position (x,y)(x,y) by a pointer device.

Example Autumn Environment.

To illustrate the Autumn language, we present a treasure-hunting environment in which an agent searches for hidden treasures using a noisy distance sensor. Figure A.1 shows the complete Autumn program implementing this environment, and Figure A.2 shows a rendered trajectory sampled from it. At the start, the environment reveals only one treasure—the gold grid cell in the middle of the grid. The agent controls a sensor probe, the grey grid cell, and moves it using four directional actions: up, down, left, and right. The top blue horizontal bar displays the probe’s noisy estimate of its distance to the nearest treasure. If the agent clicks a hidden treasure, the environment reveals it.

Appendix B AutumnBench Environment Details

This section provides detailed statistics and categorization of the AutumnBench environments. AutumnBench comprises 43 environments spanning six broad categories: 1. Physical simulations that follow intuitive, middle-school-level physics principles. 2. Emergent systems where complex patterns arise from simple rules. 3. Multi-agent dynamics that require reasoning about other agents’ goals and interactions. 4. Abstract logic environments that follow well-defined but non-physical rules. 5. Game-inspired scenarios abstracted from popular games. 6. Tool use environments that require understanding object affordances and performing multi-step reasoning.

Table B.1 reports the number of object types, #Obj; latent variables, #Latent; program length measured in lines of code; the number of event handlers, #On Clauses; stochasticity; the number of colors, #Colors; and grid size.

Appendix C AutumnBench Challenge Formulation

This section provides the formal definitions of the three challenge types in AutumnBench: masked frame prediction, change detection, and planning. For each challenge type, we define the task structure, scoring function, and empirical difficulty measurements using a random agent baseline.

To characterize task difficulty, we evaluate a random agent that selects uniformly among six action types: click, up, down, left, right, and no-op. When the agent selects click, it uniformly samples a grid position. We approximate the random agent’s performance using approximately 50 samples per environment with a 1000-step timeout. For masked frame prediction tasks, the random agent selects uniformly over six answer options, yielding a chance probability of 1/6. Table E.3 reports per-environment random agent baseline results.

C.1 Masked Frame Prediction

We define each masked frame prediction task by a tuple of a fixed action sequence 𝐚=(a1,a2,…,aT)∈𝒜T\mathbf{a}=(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{T})\in\mathcal{A}^{T} and binary masks ℳ1:T\mathcal{M}_{1:T} with ℳt⊆[W]×[H]\mathcal{M}_{t}\subseteq[W]\times[H] for t=1,…,Tt=1,\ldots,T over the observable grid. Executing 𝐚\mathbf{a} in the environment produces the observation trajectory τ=(o0,o1,…,oT)\tau=(o_{0},o_{1},\ldots,o_{T}).

Masked-frame-prediction asks the agent to predict the colors in the masked region of the final observation, oT|ℳo_{T}|_{\mathcal{M}}, choosing from the candidates KK 𝒞choices={c1,c2,…,cK}\mathcal{C}_{\text{choices}}=\{c_{1},c_{2},\ldots,c_{K}\}, where each ci∈𝒞|ℳ|c_{i}\in\mathcal{C}^{|\mathcal{M}|} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} denotes the set of possible grid cell colors.

We construct each masked frame prediction task so that, for any realization of τ\tau, exactly one candidate c∗∈𝒞choicesc^{*}\in\mathcal{C}_{\text{choices}} matches the ground truth, c∗=oT|ℳc^{*}=o_{T}|_{\mathcal{M}}. This guarantees a unique correct answer even when the underlying POMDP dynamics is stochastic.

We use a simple binary accuracy metric: score=𝟙​[correct]\text{score}=\mathbbm{1}[\text{correct}].

C.2 Change Detection

We define each change detection task with an original environment ℳ\mathcal{M} and a changed environment ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime}, both written in the Autumn language. We write their transition and observation functions as (𝒯,Ω)(\mathcal{T},\Omega) and (𝒯′,Ω′)(\mathcal{T}^{\prime},\Omega^{\prime}). A boolean guard g⁡(s,a)g(s,a) in an Autumn event handler gates the change in ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime}; g⁡(s,a)g(s,a) determines when 𝒯′\mathcal{T}^{\prime} deviates from 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

We fix an initial state distribution and an action sequence 𝐚=(a1,…,aT)\mathbf{a}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{T}). Executing 𝐚\mathbf{a} in ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} produces a realized observation prefix o′0:To^{\prime}_{0:T}. We define the defect time t∗t^{*} as the first step where this realized prefix leaves the support of ℳ\mathcal{M}:

t∗=min{t≥1:ℙℳ(o0:t=o′0:t|a1:t)⏟= 0 and ℙℳ(o0:t−1=o′0:t−1|a1:t−1)⏟> 0}.t^{*}\;=\;\min\big\{t\geq 1:\underbrace{\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{M}}(o_{0:t}=o^{\prime}_{0:t}\,|\,a_{1:t})}_{=\,0}\;\text{ and }\;\underbrace{\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{M}}(o_{0:t-1}=o^{\prime}_{0:t-1}\,|\,a_{1:t-1})}_{>\,0}\big\}. (C.1)

Equivalently, t∗t^{*} is the earliest time when o′0:to^{\prime}_{0:t} has zero probability under ℳ\mathcal{M} while o′0:t−1o^{\prime}_{0:t-1} still has positive probability under ℳ\mathcal{M}. We require the guard to trigger exactly at t∗t^{*}: g⁡(st∗−1′,at∗)=trueg(s^{\prime}_{t^{*}-1},a_{t^{*}})=\text{true} and g⁡(st−1′,at)=falseg(s^{\prime}_{t-1},a_{t})=\text{false} for all t<t∗t<t^{*}.

The agent outputs a time index tt that marks the detected change.

score​(t)={0if ​t<(t∗−1),1if ​t∈{t∗−1,t∗},1.377⋅ft∗​(t)−1.178otherwise.\text{score}(t)=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }t<(t^{*}-1),\\ 1&\text{if }t\in\{t^{*}-1,\;t^{*}\},\\ 1.377\cdot f_{t^{*}}(t)-1.178&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (C.2)

We set ft∗​(t)=11−tt∗⋅e−tt∗f_{t^{*}}(t)=\frac{1}{1-\frac{t}{t^{*}}\cdot e^{-\frac{t}{t^{*}}}}; t∗t^{*} denotes the defect time. This rule gives full credit for exact or one-step-early detection and smoothly penalizes late detections.

Across our 43 change detection environments, the random agent triggers changes with mean probability 0.80 in an average of 295 steps. Twenty-four environments trigger changes with probability 1.0, while 5 environments require 900 or more steps before changes occur, and 2 environments never trigger changes within the 1000-step timeout.

C.3 Planning

We define each planning task by a goal specification (𝒮,g)(\mathcal{S},g), where 𝒮⊆[W]×[H]\mathcal{S}\subseteq[W]\times[H] indexes a subgrid, and g∈𝒞|𝒮|g\in\mathcal{C}^{|\mathcal{S}|} specifies the target colors on 𝒮\mathcal{S}. The agent must produce an action sequence 𝐚\mathbf{a} that, when executed, produces a final observation oTo_{T} that matches the goal on the subgrid, that is, oT|𝒮=go_{T}|_{\mathcal{S}}=g. We use a simple binary success metric: score=𝟙[oT|𝒮=g]\text{score}=\mathbbm{1}[\,o_{T}|_{\mathcal{S}}=g\,].

Across our 43 planning environments, the random agent reaches the goal with mean probability 0.399 in an average of 679 steps. The random agent reaches the goal with probability 1.0 in nine environments, while 13 environments remain unsolved at the 1000-step timeout.

Appendix D Implementation Details

This section provides detailed definitions of the behavioral metrics and interface implementations used in our experiments. We first define normalized perplexity and the associated area under the curve (AUC), which quantify how agents’ actions become more focused over time. We then describe the task-specific interface implementations for both the graphical user interface used by human participants and the text-based interface used by reasoning models.

D.1 Normalized Perplexity

Definition D.1 (Normalized Perplexity)

Let p⁡(a)p(a) be the empirical action distribution over an active alphabet of size KK within a sliding window. Given entropy H(p)=−∑ap(a)log2p(a)H(p)=-\sum_{a}p(a)\log_{2}p(a) and perplexity P=2H⁡(p)P=2^{H(p)}, normalized perplexity is:

Perplexitynorm=P−1K−1∈[0,1]\text{Perplexity}_{\text{norm}}=\frac{P-1}{K-1}\in[0,1] (D.1)

where KK is the number of unique actions observed in the window, including directional keys and click positions.

Definition D.2 (Area Under the Curve (AUC) of Normalized Perplexity)

The AUC of normalized perplexity is computed as:

AUC=∫01Perplexitynorm​(x)​𝑑x\text{AUC}=\int_{0}^{1}\text{Perplexity}_{\text{norm}}(x)\,dx (D.2)

where x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1] is the normalized interaction position.

Definition D.3 (Final Normalized Perplexity)

The final normalized perplexity is the value of Perplexitynorm\text{Perplexity}_{\text{norm}} evaluated at the last window of the interaction sequence.

D.2 Task Interface Implementation

We implemented distinct interfaces for human participants and reasoning models. Human participants interact with environments through a graphical user interface (GUI), while reasoning models use a text-based interface. The following sections detail the implementation of each interface type across the three task families.

D.2.1 Graphical User Interface

For the masked frame prediction task, we implemented a slider to visualize the partially masked sequence of observations, as shown in Figure D.1. The GUI displays six answer choices from which participants select their prediction. Participants submit their selection using a Submit button.

For the planning task, we display the goal state on a static grid alongside the interactive grid, with non-target regions shaded out, as shown in Figure D.2.

For the change detection task, we provide a Found change button below the interactive grid, as shown in Figure D.3. Clicking this button transitions participants to the selection phase, where they use a slider to review observations from the test phase and identify the earliest changed frame. Participants submit their selection using a Submit button.

D.2.2 Text-Based Interface

All reasoning models receive the same text-based prompts, with the system prompt shown in Figure D.4.

For the masked frame prediction task, we add two actions in the test phase: step and rewind, which allow the model to navigate through the partially masked observations. We provide six answer options as matrices of color strings, which the model selects using the choose_option_i action.

For the planning task, we provide the target configuration in the same format as the grid observation at every timestep of the test phase.

For the change detection task, we provide a Found the change action during the test phase. Once the model selects this action, we present choose_grid_i actions enumerating the observations from the test phase. After the model chooses a grid, we display it in the subsequent prompt, allowing the model to confirm its selection using the submit action.

Example prompts for all three task types are provided in Figures D.5, D.7 and D.6.

Appendix E Additional Results

This section presents experimental results that extend those given in the main paper. We present detailed per-environment scores for all agents across the three task types, analyze the relationship between computational cost and performance, examine action distribution patterns during exploration, and provide examples of model reasoning traces. These additional analyzes support and expand on the findings discussed in Section 4.2.

Table E.1 presents the average scores for change detection, masked frame prediction, and planning across all agents and environments. Building on these overall results, this section provides detailed analyses of performance-cost relationships, action distributions, and environment difficulty characterizations.

Performance versus Cost Analysis

We evaluated two additional models, Qwen3-235b-a22b-thinking-2507 and Gemini 2.5 Flash, to establish the relationship between computational cost and performance. We partitioned all AutumnBench environments into two sets: (1) environments where average agent performance strictly increased with cost, and (2) environments where performance remained constant or decreased with increasing cost.

Overall, performance improves with higher costs in 25 of the 43 environments, but remains flat or decreases in 18 environments, and none of the environments get a score of 1.0 in the least computational cost setting.

For masked frame prediction tasks, performance increases in 16 environments, including S2KT7, T5F9B, N59TE, NF5VZ, 236VK, 6JVMF, 27JBD, BT2KZ, 4CKC2, N2NTD, YS322, 83WKQ, VA6FQ, XHGKQ, 4N7BB, and DGG2C. However, in 62.7% of environments, there is no improvement regardless of additional resources.

Change detection shows the least benefit from additional computation, with performance improvements occurring in only 14 environments: NRDF6, N59TE, NF5VZ, 236VK, 27JBD, QQM74, BT2KZ, 4CKC2, N2NTD, EAHCW, 3J4Z7, 7VKTD, VZ2Q4, and JXQAW. The remaining 29 environments do not show performance gains.

Planning tasks demonstrate improvements with cost in 16 environments, including S2KT7, KFQYT, B58F3, 27JBD, VQJH6, QQM74, 9F8AJ, 7WWW9, YS322, EAHCW, 83WKQ, 3J4Z7, 7VKTD, F5W3N, JXQAW, and 4N7BB, while 27 environments show no change. Notably, certain environments, such as 27JBD, QQM74, 7VKTD, and JXQAW, consistently benefit from additional resources across multiple tasks, while environments like 27VWC, 6JKKA, K8MTQ, and 76Z75 show no improvement in any task, suggesting fundamental reasoning limitations that cannot be overcome with additional resources alone.

Action-Distribution Analysis

We provide environment-specific results on the average number of unique actions each agent takes during exploration in Table E.2. We count each distinct click position and directional action separately. For example, clicking on positions (2,3)(2,3) and (5,7)(5,7) counts as two unique click actions. This approach allows us to account for environment-specific variations, such as differences in static object positions and grid sizes within AutumnBench. We then calculate the fraction of unique actions in each category—clicks, directional actions, reset, and no-op—relative to the total number of unique actions performed by the agent.
